title: Welltower Reports $2.7B in Senior Housing Acquisitions in Third Quarter

content:
Welltower (NYSE: WELL) closed on $2.7 billion in investments and acquisitions with deals spanning 43 senior living properties in the third quarter.
The Toledo, Ohio-based real estate investment trust completed acquisitions in markets including Naples, Florida; Denver; San Jose, California; and Los Angeles, according to the company’s most recent financial disclosure.
Welltower notched an increase in its senior housing operating platform same-store revenue increasing by 9.1% year-over-year, led by 320 basis points of occupancy growth across the portfolio and a 5.3% increase in revenue per occupied room (RevPOR) in the third quarter.
In 2026, Welltower has closed or is under contract to close $21 billion in investments, with $13.3 billion completed in the first three quarters across its entire portfolio. The remaining $7.7 billion is expected to close through the final quarter of the year.
Welltower’s net operating income (NOI) rose 15.8% in the last 12 months, and management attributes that to higher revenue in from the senior housing operating portfolio. Welltower management reported a 21% increase in same-store net operating income in the third quarter of 2026 compared to the same period last year.
Alongside the acquisitions and investments, Welltower shed 25 outpatient medical buildings and seven senior housing properties in the third quarter to generate an additional $284 million in revenue.
Also on the disposition front, Brookdale (NYSE: BKD) acquired 30 communities it leased and operated from Welltower for $290 million.
As a result of the investment activity and performance of the REIT’s portfolio, annual guidance has been revised to a range of $3.31 to $3.37 per diluted share from the previous range of $3.11 to $3.19.
Earlier this year, leadership at Welltower announced the company secured $6.2 billion in acquisitions, most of which were sourced off-market.
Welltower’s stock is priced at $240.61 per share, up 1.4% from the previous close.

title: Now the Largest U.S. Senior Living Operator, Discovery Makes Good on Growth Thesis
description: This story is part of your SHN+ subscription Discovery Senior Living is officially the nation’s largest senior living operator. It’s set to grow even larger in the coming years. The company just announced the planned acquisition of Sunshine Retirement Living, which will help set the stage for future growth in the Pacific Northwest. content:
This story is part of your SHN+ subscription
Discovery Senior Living is officially the nation’s largest senior living operator. It’s set to grow even larger in the coming years.
The company just announced the planned acquisition of Sunshine Retirement Living, which will help set the stage for future growth in the Pacific Northwest. For Sunshine, joining the Discovery ecosystem gives access to technology and corporate support without losing sight of the company’s strong operating culture built over the last 15 years, Sunshine President Luis Serrano said.
Discovery Senior Living blazed a unique trail in the industry by growing using a strategy that helped companies like hotel management firm Aimbridge Hospitality expand. The company’s portfolio is organized into multiple smaller operating companies with brands and operations geared toward their respective markets.
The Sunshine acquisition makes Hutchinson’s priorities from earlier this year a reality by building density in new markets and expanding Discovery’s business intelligence platform.
“We’re actually seeing the thesis play out now,” Hutchinson said during an interview with Senior Housing News at the Fall NIC conference in Chicago . “As we grow in the segmentation model and the separated Manco model infused with all this data and analytics, we’re accelerating performance.”
Leaders with the Bonita Springs, Florida-based senior living provider also are honing the company’s approach to middle-market communities and communities in secondary markets after launching a four-tier operating structure in July.
These efforts serve as the next stage of an evolving operating model that Hutchinson and the Discovery executive leadership team built over the last decade. Now, they see a critical challenge translating national resources into stronger operating performance without losing an edge in local market appeal that makes communities part of its 10 regional management companies successful.
Discovery is now the largest senior living provider and the largest private senior living provider in the country with 420 communities under management spanning 47,000 units in 40 states.
The distinction as the country’s largest senior living provider “puts more responsibility” on Discovery to “help lead and provide considerations for others” while also “taking some chances that we can afford to take” given the company’s scale, Hutchinson said.
“The designation is less important and a waypoint on a journey that’s going to continue,” Hutchinson said.
Sunshine acquisition sets stage for growth
With the Sunshine acquisition, Discovery’s leaders are following a strategy they have spent years honing. The acquisition of Integral Senior Living in 2023 and the consecutive launches of regional operating companies such as Arvum Senior Living, LakeHouse Senior Living and Provincial Senior Living.
To succeed in the Pacific Northwest, a region densely populated with older adults and an area that dates its senior living roots back to the industry’s early days, Hutchinson said Discovery needed “scale and mass,” rather than pursuing one-off transactions to establish a patchwork foothold in the region.
The Sunshine acquisition sets the stage for future growth in the region with an operating partner that older adults in the Pacific Northwest trust. This approach mirrors Discovery’s rationale behind the ISL acquisition in 2023, in that the company is acquiring an intact platform managed by a specialized operator able to navigate stringent state and federal regulations.
Preserving Sunshine’s culture, brand and community relationships was “essential” in making the transaction possible, Sunshine President Luis Serrano told SHN. Going forward, Sunshine will operate its communities, maintain branding and culture that older adults have been accustomed to in the past now with the scale and corporate support of Discovery at play.
Having experienced leaders within regional management companies matters for Hutchinson, and Serrano fits that mold, he noted. Luis Serrano and his late wife, May Sunshine Hasso Serrano, founded the operator in 2009 to manage a portfolio of communities following the Holiday Retirement sale to Fortress Investment Group in 2007. Serrano brings experience from management consulting work with McKinsey & Company and JPMorgan Chase, and he was the senior vice president of business and corporate development for telecommunications company Boingo Wireless during its effort to go public on the NASDAQ in 2011.
The Sunshine-Discovery transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of this year, and the company’s project management department and its dozen-member business assimilation team will work with Sunshine communities to handle their transition. This includes moving contracts, coordinating systems and managing an overlap period where leadership and community teams gain access to Discovery’s corporate support and business intelligence resources.
This strike team to help Sunshine communities join Discovery is emblematic of the company’s past growth, keeping operational decisions closer to the community level and shifting the administrative burden to executive leaders tasked with “removing the friction” transitions can sometimes bring, Hutchinson noted.
In 2027, Hutchinson sees an important test ahead for the industry in balancing the pursuit of stronger operating performance with the growing complexity of risk, regulation and public scrutiny on the sector. Workforce issues remain a persistent challenge, but beyond staffing, Hutchinson believes operators must pay more attention to protecting the performance they are working to improve.
Managing risk and maintaining an operating model that can easily explain financial metrics and operating dynamics to interested institutional investors will also be key in 2027 and beyond, Hutchinson told Senior Housing News.
Hutchinson, who also serves as chair of the American Seniors Housing Association, sees an opening for the industry to build stronger connections between state and federal advocacy as public scrutiny of senior living grows. He said that during ASHA’s strategic planning process in 2026, member companies identified coordination and education as important priorities to inform lawmakers and the public on senior living. Moving the industry forward will also require changes in how policymakers and consumers understand senior living, Hutchinson said.
“This is going to be a decades-long conversation,” Hutchinson said. “But we need to start recognizing the differences, and then proactively creating that connectivity.”
Data overhaul shifts from setting the foundation to execution
Discovery’s leaders are overhauling the company’s data and business intelligence systems to improve performance while creating a technology ecosystem that can share data across communities. The goal is to give regional leaders actionable data on a real-time rather than on a trailing basis.
This spring, the company’s technology ecosystem included 22 platforms, and the company is whittling down that number by creating a data lake via technology company Snowflake that brings information from all systems into a shared environment which can give more insight into financial performance, clinical outcomes and resident engagement that can then be used by communities to fit their needs.
Earlier this year, Discovery appointed Tom Costello as chief performance officer, tying the technology effort to its operating priorities of strong performance and resident satisfaction, Hutchinson said.
Discovery is now further along in its technology journey to combine information from different reporting systems and is making informed business intelligence decisions possible at the local level, Hutchinson said.
Instead of requiring new operating companies or acquired communities to adopt the same software, Discovery can pull data into its data lake from existing operating systems without the need for an operator to overhaul its range of technology partners. Using a three-tier data “cleansing process,” Discovery’s growing IT team takes community-level data and transforms it into common business terms that can be understood across communities and property types in digestible reports.
Discovery is also exploring AI applications in marketing, customer service and pattern recognition in analytics. The ability to retrofit a data infrastructure into an operator’s existing technology ecosystem prepares the company for a time in which institutional investors demand more sophisticated financial and operational reporting, Hutchinson added.
“Our thesis is that as more sophisticated capital comes into this space, you’re going to get a lot more stress on being able to provide that data-backed decision-making model,” Hutchinson said.
Segmentation, operations set up next phase of growth
In 2027, Discovery is focused on matching community services, staffing and spending to specific cohorts of older adults as they seek out senior living, and this matches up with the company’s horizontal growth model to understand local market dynamics, Hutchinson said.
As seen in the company’s market-by-market approach for setting resident rental rates and lean operating models prioritizing back-end support for its regional management companies, Discovery reorganized its brands into select, classic, premium and distinguished tiers in July.
These segments take into consideration differences in revenue potential, resident rates, staffing, care complexity, services and physical amenities. Alongside these changes in how brands are tiered, Discovery is working on operating guidelines that match services with what residents in different communities want and can afford to pay.
“You get better when you have a more bespoke and customized playbook based on the needs and desires of your customer,” Hutchinson said.
He sees opportunity in changing how Discovery organizes operations across smaller communities, and a small-community operating playbook is under development that focuses on activities and operations, instead of treating each community as a separate operating unit. The premise behind this is to create a different economic profile for middle-market communities, where the ability to generate a return is still needed to attract capital investment, Hutchinson said.
“We’re going to continue to build on this,” Hutchinson said. “We’re going to continue to take care of as many seniors as humanly possible.”
Fueling all of this is an emphasis on leadership development and staffing. In 2023, Discovery announced plans for a learning and training center, and now the company is working to further career development opportunities for motivated leaders across the company. Discovery is taking lessons from hospitality and other industries as it looks for ways to improve retention and create practical advancement opportunities across its web of regional management companies.
Discovery has almost 28,000 employees, Hutchinson said. Through September, thousands had volunteered to participate in self-advancement coursework during their own time.
“Inside of your workforce are your next leaders,” Hutchinson said. “I am convinced of that.”

title: Not a Full Wave: Inside Green Street’s Senior Living Development Forecast
description: Senior living stakeholders are indeed moving ahead with new projects in 2026, mostly on the high end of the senior living market. But don’t call it a full development wave. Companies such as American House Senior Living and Brightview Senior Living are right now assembling development pipelines. At the same time, Sunrise Senior Living is […] The post Not a Full Wave: Inside Green Street’s Senior Living Development Forecast appeared first on Senior Housing News .
content:
Senior living stakeholders are indeed moving ahead with new projects in 2026, mostly on the high end of the senior living market. But don’t call it a full development wave.
Companies such as American House Senior Living and Brightview Senior Living are right now assembling development pipelines. At the same time, Sunrise Senior Living is embarking on a $7.5 billion, 50-community development push.
Making this possible is the fact that development fundamentals currently favor high-end projects that can charge the rent necessary for them to pencil out.
A Green Street report from September showed yields on new Class A communities in 2026 of about 8%, which translates into roughly 30% development profit margins with a capitalization rate near 6%. Communities with per-unit rent closer to average would have to earn thousands of dollars more in revenue per occupied room (RevPOR) in order to pencil out, the data showed.
As high-end projects pencil out, more companies will seek to develop them, according to Michael Stroyeck, Head of US Health Care Research at Green Street.
“Development should begin picking up,” Stroyeck told Senior Housing News. “I think we’ll see a modest acceleration in starts next year.”
But a full development wave this is not. While high-end projects pencil out in 2026, middle-market communities and those with more modest rent profiles still do not. The Green Street report’s authors wrote that, for average communities, “rents are still well below levels needed to generate a sufficient return on cost and incentivize investors to take on development risk.”
Green Street and Stroyeck have revised their senior living growth forecast lower and now expect about 1% of total senior living supply growth in 2029 and 3% of senior living supply growth in 2030.
“Development is picking up, but there are a lot of reasons that the supply floodgates aren’t going to just completely open up overnight,” he said. “You need very high-single-digits to low-double-digits type rents per month on a continuum-of-care type product, and there are a lot of markets out there that just simply can’t afford that.”
As average senior living communities remain tough to pencil, investors and developers are flocking to data centers, which carry higher development returns and lower risk relative to senior housing. There is also the fact that senior living is such an operating-intensive business, and that developers now need seasoned operators in tow to get financing for projects, among other issues acting as barriers to new development.
There also is simply more room to grow in high-end senior living. Industry data cited by Green Street’s Stroyeck showed that a median-income older adult can afford about six years of senior living on average.
As many as 40% to 45% of older adults in the median-income range for the U.S. can afford the average cost of senior housing as it is today. That will help fuel more high-end development in the months and years to come.
“There’s a large tail at that wealthy end of this industry,” Stroyek said.
For now, senior living stakeholders still are figuring out how to make middle-market projects work. Green Street and Stroyek ran the math on what an operator would need to charge to hit 30% profit margins: A community, even one with a continuum of care, would have to charge $7,000 to $8,000 per month. That is still a sizable gap over what communities can charge in primary and secondary markets across the country.
“We’re expecting mid-single-digit market rent growth over our entire forecast period through 2030. So, I think you will get there, but it’s also going to depend on what happens with construction costs, and that’s a big unknown in today’s environment,” Stroyek added.

title: The operational value of cognitive care
description: When a resident’s cognitive-communication function changes and that change is affecting daily activities, an SLP referral should be an automatic part of the response.
content:
In many skilled nursing facilities, supervision needs creep up quietly. A resident who previously completed dressing with only set-up assistance now needs repeated verbal cues to locate items and finish the task. Another is physically able to transfer but cannot remember how to do so safely. A third resident can participate in familiar tasks, but only when someone provides step-by-step directions.
These cognitive changes can gradually become part of the care routine before anyone stops to ask two critical questions: What changed, and was the resident referred to the speech-language pathologist?
Cognitive-communication deficits can affect attention, memory, reasoning, problem solving, executive function, safety awareness and the ability to follow directions. When those deficits interfere with a resident’s ability to carry out daily routines, use compensatory strategies, communicate needs or make safe choices, the impact is felt by the resident and the entire care team.
A resident may appropriately need increased assistance because of a chronic condition or progressive decline. But a new, worsening or previously unevaluated change in cognitive-communication function can also signal a skilled, medically necessary need that should be assessed and treated.
That clinical need has operational implications. A resident who needs fewer verbal cues, check-ins or hands-on assists frees care team time for other priorities. The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association’s (ASHA) Cognitive Treatment in Skilled Nursing Facilities snapshot, based on data from ASHA’s National Outcomes Measures System (NOMS), found that 35% to 48% of patients receiving cognitive-communication treatment from a speech-language pathologist (SLP) required less supervision or assistance because of cognitive deficits.
The data also show that a greater proportion of patients who received 11 or more treatment sessions made progress in cognitive communication compared with patients who received one to 10 sessions.
When to refer to an SLP
These findings support a practical leadership premise: When a resident’s cognitive-communication function changes and that change is affecting daily activities, an SLP referral should be an automatic part of the response.
That starts with the people closest to the resident. The nursing, dietary and activities team members are often the first to notice that a resident is having more difficulty with a familiar task, remembering a safety strategy or communicating a need. They do not need to determine why the change occurred. But they do need to know what to observe and how to refer the resident to the SLP.
Facilities can support that process by sharing ASHA’s SLP Referral Guidelines for Skilled Nursing Facilities with the care team. The form identifies cognitive-communication changes that warrant an SLP referral. ASHA’s On the Radar: Quick Referral Trainings for Long-Term Care Teams can also help reinforce when to involve the SLP through short training sessions. Together, these resources help the care team feel more confident about when to make a referral.
The most useful referrals describe the change and its functional effect. “Needs more help” signals that something has changed, but it does not identify the barrier. “Now requires repeated verbal cues to begin grooming, cannot locate items without assistance, and leaves the task unfinished” gives the SLP and the interdisciplinary team a clearer clinical starting point.
For facility leaders, the opportunity is straightforward: Make an SLP referral part of the response when a resident’s level of assistance changes. An assessment may identify skilled treatment and individualized strategies that help the resident complete daily activities more safely and independently.
The downstream return is meaningful. When a resident needs fewer cues, less frequent check-ins or decreased levels of supervision, teams have more time to respond to another resident’s needs, complete required care tasks and address other priorities in the flow of care.
Ashley Haltenhof, MS, CCC-SLP, CADDCT, CDP, is director of healthcare services in speech-language pathology for the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA). Prior to ASHA, Ashley’s career was focused on clinical development and operations in post-acute care settings.

title: ケアマネの就業・退職、事業者に届け出を義務化　10日以内に都道府県へ　厚労省方針
description: 厚生労働省は26日の審議会（社会保障審議会・介護保険部会）で、ケアマネジャーを雇用する事業者に「従事届」「非従事届」（いずれも仮称）の提出を新たに義務付ける方針を示した。【Joint編集部】 ケアマネジャー資格の更新制の […]
content:
厚生労働省は26日の審議会（社会保障審議会・介護保険部会）で、ケアマネジャーを雇用する事業者に「従事届」「非従事届」（いずれも仮称）の提出を新たに義務付ける方針を示した。【Joint編集部】
ケアマネジャー資格の更新制の廃止後、新たに受講を求めていく研修の対象者を把握する仕組みとして導入する。ケアマネジャーの配置が必要な全てのサービスの事業者を対象とする。
「従事届」「非従事届」の提出が義務付けられるのは次の場合だ。
● 従事届：新たにケアマネジャーを業務に従事させた場合
● 非従事届：ケアマネジャーが退職した場合や、病気、災害、育児、親族の介護といったやむを得ない事情により、一定期間、研修の受講が難しくなる場合
厚労省は今回、こうした事実が生じた日から10日以内に都道府県へ報告することを義務付けると説明した。
更新制の廃止後も、実務に従事するケアマネジャーには引き続き研修の受講を求めていく方針だ。ただし、離職中のケアマネジャーらはこうした研修の受講対象から除外されるため、事業者からの報告を通じて従事状況などを確認する狙いがある。
事業者にはこのほか、雇用しているケアマネジャーが研修を受けられる機会を確保することも義務付けられる。勤務時間中の受講を労働時間として扱うことや、円滑に学べるよう業務配分・人員配置を調整することなどが想定されている。
この日の審議会では委員から、小規模な事業者への支援や事務負担の軽減などを促す声があがった。更新制の廃止と新たな研修体系への移行は、2027年12月1日に施行される。

title: ケアマネ法定研修、「更新」から「定期」へ　時間数どう変わる？　厚労省が新体系を提示
description: 「更新研修」から「定期研修」へ ーー 。厚生労働省は26日の審議会（社会保障審議会・介護保険部会）で、ケアマネジャー資格の更新制の廃止に伴う法定研修の新たな体系を明らかにした。【Joint編集部】 更新制の廃止後、現場で […]
content:
「更新研修」から「定期研修」へ ーー 。厚生労働省は26日の審議会（社会保障審議会・介護保険部会）で、ケアマネジャー資格の更新制の廃止に伴う法定研修の新たな体系を明らかにした。【Joint編集部】
更新制の廃止後、現場で実務に従事しているケアマネジャーに受講を義務付ける各種研修について、名称や時間数を次のように見直す。
● 現行の「専門Ⅰ課程」は「初任研修」に変更。56時間から42時間に短縮する。
● 現行の「専門Ⅱ課程」と「更新研修（実務経験者）」は「定期研修」に再編。現行の「専門Ⅱ課程」や2回目以降の「更新研修」と同じ32時間とする。
● 現行の「主任介護支援専門員更新研修」は「主任介護支援専門員定期研修」に変更。46時間を維持する。
「初任研修」と「定期研修」を合わせて、就業後の最初の5年間に受ける研修は計74時間。厚労省は現行の88時間から14時間短縮し、ケアマネジャーの負担軽減を図る。
「初任研修」については、就業後6ヵ月以上3年以内の受講を求める。離職中や育休中などの期間は、この6ヵ月以上3年以内に算入しない。
「定期研修」は原則、5年ごとを一区切りとして受講する決まりとする方針。オンライン・オンデマンドが基本で、ケアマネジャーがそれぞれのタイミングで分割して受講できるようにする。
更新制の廃止の施行日は2027年12月1日。同日から新たな研修体系へ移行する。
summary: 「更新研修」から「定期研修」へ ーー 。● 現行の「専門Ⅰ課程」は「初任研修」に変更。56時間から42時間に短縮する。● 現行の「主任介護支援専門員更新研修」は「主任介護支援専門員定期研修」に変更。

主任ケアマネジャーも含めて資格の更新制をなくす。介護支援専門員証は有効期限を撤廃し、恒久化する。
厚労省は一方で、実務に従事するケアマネジャーに引き続き定期的な研修の受講を義務付ける。

厚労省はあわせて、施行時点で既にケアマネジャーとして働いている人の研修の受講について、次の取り扱いとする方針を示した。

● 来年度に旧制度の研修（専門Ⅱ・更新・主任更新）を修了した人は、2030年3月末まで受講を免除する。その後、5年ごとを一区切りに研修を受講することとする。
資格の更新制が廃止され、新たな研修体系に移行するのは来年12月1日。この施行日前に介護支援専門員証の有効期限を迎える人は、従来どおり期限までに更新研修を受講する必要がある。

2026年10月23日
特養の55.8%が赤字 全国老施協「介護崩壊と言うべき危険水域」 昨年度決算調査
全国老人福祉施設協議会は23日、特別養護老人ホームの経営状況などを明らかにする「収支状況等調査」の結果を公表した。【Joint編集部】
昨年度決算の速報値で、回答した1582施設の55.8%が赤字だったと報告した。
2015年度の時点で既に32.4%だった特養の赤字施設の割合は、この10年間で一段と悪化。昨年度は半数を超える水準に至った。
平均の収支差率も、10年前の2015年度はプラス2.7%だったが、昨年度はマイナス0.8%に落ち込んでいる。
＊ 赤字施設の割合と平均の収支差率は、いずれも補助金を除く。
全国老施協はこのほか、人件費や事業費、事務費、水道光熱費などの増加が、長期的にみて、介護報酬のプラス改定による収入増を上回っていることを示すデータも公表。公定価格のもとで価格転嫁も難しく、個々の施設の経営努力だけでは限界があると訴えた。
全国老施協の大山知子会長は今月、こうした実態を踏まえて厚生労働省へ要望書を提出。「事業の休止、廃止、廃業が急増している。介護崩壊と言うべき危険水域に達している」との危機感を直に伝えた。
要望書では来年度の介護報酬改定に向けて、「基本報酬の大胆な底上げ」を強く求めた。これに加えて、
● 今後の物価・賃金の上昇を見込んだ十分な対応
● 介護従事者の他職種と遜色のない処遇改善
● 食費・居住費の基準費用額の引き上げ
などの実現も働きかけた。

title: 【和田誠】介護報酬が上がれば、現場は救われるのか　介護保険は誰のもの？ 「サービス控え」を生まないために
description: 介護現場の人手不足を解消し、介護職員の処遇改善を進めるために、「介護報酬の引き上げ」を求める声が高まっています。【和田誠】 確かに、現場を支えるホームヘルパーや介護職員の処遇改善は一刻の猶予も許されない課題です。 しかし […]
content:
【和田誠】介護報酬が上がれば、現場は救われるのか 介護保険は誰のもの？ 「サービス控え」を生まないために
介護現場の人手不足を解消し、介護職員の処遇改善を進めるために、「介護報酬の引き上げ」を求める声が高まっています。【和田誠】
確かに、現場を支えるホームヘルパーや介護職員の処遇改善は一刻の猶予も許されない課題です。
しかし、ここで一度立ち止まって考えてみてください。事業所に支払われる介護報酬だけを引き上げたとき、サービスを利用する当事者や家族の暮らしには何が起きるのでしょうか？
◆ 単価引き上げで生じる「利用量の目減り」
介護保険制度は、利用者が尊厳を保持し、住み慣れた地域で自立した日常生活を営むための不可欠な社会基盤です。
しかし、在宅介護を支える基本サービス費や加算が引き上げられても、それを受けるための枠組みである「区分支給限度基準額」が、そのまま据え置かれたとしたらどうでしょう？
各サービスの単価（介護報酬）が上がれば、限度額の枠内で利用できるサービスの「量」は実質的に目減りしてしまいます。限度額を超えて全額を自己負担するか、さもなければ必要なデイサービスや訪問介護の利用回数を減らすしかありません。
すでに長引く在宅介護の中で、「いつまで貯金を取り崩せるのか」「離職して自分が抱え込むしかないのか」などと限界まで追い詰められている当事者世帯にとって、これは単なる計算問題ではないのです。
◆ ケアの質と量を減らさないために
介護報酬の引き上げが、結果として当事者の経済的負担を増やし、「サービス控え」や「利用断念」を引き起こしてしまう。これでは、適切な在宅ケアをあきらめざるを得なくなり、結果として「介護の質」も「介護の量」も損なわれてしまうのではないでしょうか？
ケアの担い手を守るための改定が、ケアを受ける当事者を追い詰めることになってよいはずがありません。介護の質と量を決して減らさないために、制度はどうあるべきなのでしょうか？
◆ 処遇改善と「区分支給限度基準額の引き上げ」を両輪に
「認知症の人と家族の会」は、国の審議会（社会保障審議会・介護給付費分科会）に対して、来年度の介護報酬改定に向けた要望書を提出しました。
職員の抜本的な処遇改善とともに、利用者が経済的な理由でケアをあきらめずに済むよう、「区分支給限度基準額の適切な引き上げ」と「低所得者層へのきめ細かな負担軽減策」を、同時に検討することを強く求めています。
現場で働く人を支えることと、当事者の暮らしを守ること。この両輪をいかに成り立たせるのか、今まさに制度の真価が問われています。

介護現場の人手不足を解消し、介護職員の処遇改善を進めるために、「介護報酬の引き上げ」を求める声が高まっています。◆ ケアの質と量を減らさないために

見直し案では例えば、事故の原因分析と再発防止策を整理して記載できるよう、記入欄の構成が変更された。自由記載が中心だった従来の形式から、次の7つの観点ごとに項目を設ける形に改められている。
● 利用者の行為・状態変化
● 組織運営体制
● マニュアル・手順
● 環境・設備
● 介護技術
● 職員間の連携・情報共有
● その他

昨年12月にまとめられた審議会（社会保障審議会・介護保険部会）の意見書を踏まえた取り組み。全国の事故の情報を収集し、その傾向や原因などを分析したうえで、得られた知見を現場に還元するサイクルを作ることで、再発防止とサービスの質の向上につなげる狙いがある。

厚生労働省は22日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた議論を進めている有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、生活介護の具体策を取り上げた。【Joint編集部】
特別支援学校を卒業した後の居場所や学習機会などを確保し、本人が障害児から障害者へと移り変わった後も、支援を切れ目なくつなぐための施策を提案した。
背景には、学校の卒業を境に必要な支援が十分に受けられなくなるとの指摘がある。
学齢期は通学や放課後等デイサービスなどで、夕方も含めて居場所、余暇活動、学習・社会参加の機会などが確保されている。ただし、卒業してから生活介護を利用するようになると、サービス提供時間や活動内容が違うため状況が変わってしまう。
働いている家族からは、夕方以降の居場所や預かりが課題だという声が上がっているほか、人との交流も含めた生涯学習の機会が十分に確保されないとの意見もある。
厚労省は今回、家族の負担軽減も念頭に次の対応策を提案した。
● 延長支援加算の評価を拡充する。その際、強度行動障害のある人や医療的ケアを必要とする人など、重度障害者への評価も拡充する。
● 生活介護事業所と日中一時支援事業所などが連携して支援するケースを新たに評価する。
● 生活介護事業所での生涯学習の実施を努力義務に位置付ける。
今後、具体的な評価や運営ルールのあり方などについてさらに検討を深める。来年度改定に向けて、年末にも施策の大枠を固める予定だ。

content:
2026年10月21日
デイサービスの送迎、年間100万円超の赤字 全国老施協が試算 基本報酬の増額など訴える
全国老人福祉施設協議会がデイサービスの送迎の実態を明らかにする調査結果を新たに公表した。【Joint編集部】
介護職員の平均給与に基づく人件費などで試算すると、送迎部分だけで1事業所あたり年間100万円超の赤字が出ると報告した。
今回、全国老施協はデイサービス事業所の収入、運行状況、車両費用、人件費などをもとに送迎の収支を試算した。
今年1月の実績をもとに年間の収支を試算すると、人件費に介護職員の平均給与を用いた場合は、1事業所あたりおよそ115万円の赤字となった。全産業平均の給与水準を用いると、およそ229万円の赤字だった。ガソリン代や修理・整備費、人件費の増加などが背景にある。
全国老施協は今月14日、通所介護や地域密着型通所介護などが取り上げられた審議会（社会保障審議会・介護給付費分科会）に要望書を提出。来年度の介護報酬改定で、実態に合った送迎の評価を実現するよう強く求めた。
要望書では、基本報酬に包括化されている片道47単位という送迎の基本的な評価が、2003年から長く変わっていないと問題を提起。次のような改善策の実現を訴えた。
● 基本報酬の引き上げと送迎減算の見直し
● 特別地域加算、中山間地域等における小規模事業所加算の通所系サービスへの適用
今回の全国老施協の調査は、今年3月から5月にかけて会員を対象に行われたもの。全国963のデイサービス事業所から回答を得ている。

Claude Haiku 5.5
7th October 2026
As previously promised, here’s Anthropic’s new fast, low cost model: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5.
The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago, and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output—relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, released last month.
The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna—$0.10/$0.50—up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75.
Haiku 5.5 also uses a new, less generous tokenizer. My Claude Token Counter tool shows that the same long prompt uses around 1.25x as many tokens with Haiku 5.5 compared to Haiku 4.5, so there’s a hidden price increase there.
If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal.
The most recent release of llm-anthropic finally fixed it so I don’t need to ship a new version of that plugin for every new model. I tested the new model like this:
llm install -U llm-anthropic
llm anthropic refresh
llm -m claude-haiku-5.5 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" -o thinking_effort low
Pelicans
Here are pelicans for low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. The new Haiku doesn’t let you disable reasoning, and defaults to medium
. I got a good bicycle frame for everything beyond low
. The low effort pelican cost 0.0936 cents and took 7 seconds.
This max
effort pelican (with a reasoning trace that starts “This is the classic pelican-on-bicycle SVG test...”) took 5 minutes 9 seconds to generate, but still only cost me 3.3826 cents:
(Since the reasoning trace exhibits awareness of the benchmark, here’s Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars (on xhigh), and the same prompt against some other recent models. Background on that.)
For comparison, here’s the pelican I got a year ago from Haiku 4.5 (for 0.7583 cents—Haiku 4.5 did not support reasoning levels). It sucked at drawing pelicans:
And a generous API credit scheme for subscribers
In addition to Haiku 5.5, Anthropic announced today that they are halving the price of cache reads for Sonnet 5.5. They’ve also added API credits to subscription plans:
Second, this week, we’ll roll out a new monthly API credit to all Max and Team subscribers for use on the Claude Platform. Max 5x users will get $100 in credits per month, Max 20x users will get $200, and Team subscribers will receive up to $500, pooled across their users.
Claiming this is pleasantly easy: navigate to Settings -> Billing and select the API organization that should benefit from the credits every month:
The API credits exactly match the cost of the subscription itself. This is really generous—it makes it much easier for subscribers to use the API. Anthropic also let you disable auto-reload for the API, with the consequence that “API requests will stop when your balance runs out”—exactly what you want if you’re planning to burn through those API credits without risk of a nasty billing surprise.
Note that the monthly credits do not roll over—use them or lose them.
OpenAI still allow you to use your Codex subscription for personal API use, which works out as a better deal for heavy API users. This new credit scheme goes at least some way to overcoming that difference.

description: I'm at OpenAI DevDay today, in Fort Mason, San Francisco. Same as last year I'll be live blogging the keynote and some other notes during the day. content:
OpenAI DevDay 2026 live blog
29th September 2026
I’m at OpenAI DevDay today, in Fort Mason, San Francisco. Same as last year I’ll be live blogging the keynote and some other notes during the day.
OpenAI gave me a free ticket and a seat in the “creator” area for the keynote.
09:27 I'm in the room for the keynote, which starts in half an hour.
This year I vibe-coded a system for more easily adding photos to my live blog. I intended to do that using Codex Cloud (I built it on my phone on the way to the venue) but ran into problems with that and switched to Claude Code for web instead.
10:01 Sam Altman is on stage, welcoming us to DevDay. He promises "our best DevDay yet".
10:02 Showing features they've shipped that people asked for. Codex on Linux and Codex on your phone both got some applause.
10:03 Today, a product to feel like a "whole new way of working with AI". My guess is that it's a personal agent similar to Muse...
10:03
10:03 It's called "Dots".
10:05 It does look very Muse-like. You get to pick its name, then it's represented by a cute blob-like avatar. (My Muse avatar is a pelican.)
10:06 This demo video includes a whole lot of voice interactions, presumably using GPT-Live or a new generation of that technology.
10:06
10:07 Dots are "powered by Astra". That would be an expensive default model!
10:08 A very ambitious use-case, migrating an API. I'm surprised that they went for such a code-heavy example so early on, I guess this is a developer audience.
10:09 Sam called Astra "our most aligned model", to allow you to trust your Dot with "as much responsibility as you are comfortable with".
10:09 "You also need a place four your team to collaborate with their Dots". So they are introducing ChatGPT Space.
10:10
These Spaces look like shared artifacts, maybe Google Docs meets the artifacts pattern.
Sam Introduces Holly Li.
10:11 Holly is talking through a scenario building fictional music app. Holly has a Dot called "Dottie", which has access to ChatGPT, Slack, Teams, and more.
10:12 This UI really does look like Meta's Muse agent, currently still at number one on the iOS App Store free list.
10:13 Live demo! "Dottie is having a slow morning" - we got a "still checking" and an embarrassing silent moment.
10:14 Now we're in ChatGPT Space. It has a Notion-style slash menu.
10:16 People at OpenAI started delegating to their Dots directly in Slack, which have their own identities in OpenAI Slack. I guess this is OpenAI's answer to Claude Tag.
10:17 "Dottie can use Codex on my laptop to build the app and launch it in the iPhone Simulator."
10:18 ChatGPT Pro and Enterprise customers get access to Dots today.
10:19
10:19 They're also building "specialist dots" for legal, finance, etc. They'll collaborate with enterprises on this, and are also doing a thing with Microsoft 365 around these.
10:20 "The second big part of today" is about platforms. Says says: Great models. Tools - access to the same tools used within OpenAI. And distribution.
10:21 People have been asking for GPT-6 Astra but cheaper and faster. Today they're launching GPT-6.1 Sol.
10:21 "Near-Astra level intelligence at a fifth of the price".
10:22 6.1 Sol is launching by today.
10:22 Also today: Ultrafast. 8x faster - up to 300 tokens/second. Available in the API, ChatGPT, and Codex. 6x the price of standard - "you know what, it's worth it" says Sam.
10:22 Ultrafast is available for Astra 6 today, and Sol 6.1 soon.
10:23 New subscription plan: Pro 500. This gives you access to Ultrafast, and 25x the usage of Plus. They're also putting their $200/month plan back on sale for new subscribers today.
10:24 Also today: previewing a new Decisions API. Lets the model respond "in a fraction of a second". It works by giving the Luna model "a predefined set of options to choose from". Sounds like their response to Jev, which came out of stealth less than two weeks ago!
10:25 Sam is now talking about Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI. He brings up Tejal Patwardhan to talk about how they're using their own models to accelerate their research.
10:26 Tejal is talking about Astra's abilities at Computer Use. "Our models helped optimize the harness we use for Computer Use". They accelerated the harness, getting "a 2x latency win that we've shipped to all of you".
10:27 "Our models are much less likely to make a mistake while navigating the desktop and the browser" - which "should really matter for all your Dots".
10:28
10:29 Sam is back. Now talking about "supporting developers" - giving developers access to the same foundations they have at OpenAI. This starts with the open source Codex harness. Codex is also now "fully in the cloud". I had a bad experience with Codex in the cloud just two hours ago, so hopefully this new launch will make that a whole lot better.
10:30 Today launching "Codex Security Cloud", with "Daybreak Blue access" - scheduled scans, automatic de-duplication. Also launched today.
10:31 There's a (new?) Agents API, now with Computer Use.
10:31 (My eyes glazed over a bit at the AWS partnership section, but it only lasted a few seconds.)
10:32 Sam is dashing through a section about enterprise privacy features.
10:33 Sam is boasting about the "most performant and reliable API" available today. Feels like a jab at Claude, especially given they had an outage just this morning.
10:33 Romain Huet just made a fun entrance, with a live demo as he walked into the venue (with camera footage on screen.)
10:34 Looks like he's going to show off some 3D modeling with Ultrafast, in a live demo. The voice mode is not collaborating! He's going to have to type instead.
10:35
10:36 This is a good demo. He's typing commands like "put the livestream on the big screen" and a moment later the video appears on the big screen in the 3D model of the venue.
10:38 Romain is live coding an app to distribute free tickets to random attendees, using Ultrafast.
10:39 (This fits a pattern - in previous DevDays Romain has frequently run live demos that interact with the audience in interesting ways.)
10:39 Now we have an Astra Computer Use demo, where Astra figures out how to play a new (vibe coded) game.
10:40
10:41 ... and a demo showing Codex Remote building an app for the iPhone Duo, showing the UI from the simulator in the Codex UI.
10:42 Now Romain is switching to Codex Cloud, with "rewrite the entire backend in Rust".
10:43 Last demo, this time using Hugging Face Microduck robot.
10:44
10:46 Sam is back. 1.2B people use ChatGPT every week. "We've tried this before with variable results", but they're trying this again. First up: sign in with ChatGPT, which lets people sign into your app and use the tokens they are paying for already. I've wanted this one for years!
10:46 Also: Plugin extensions - plugins that are "entire applications" that feel native to ChatGPT (and Codex).
10:47 Here's an sample ChatGPT plugin from Adobe.
10:48 You can also build ChatGPT Sites and share them with specific other people. (I admit I thought they had that feature already.)
10:49 And they're launching the OpenAI Marketplace today, with these partners.
10:49 Finishing with a feel-good bit profiling some people who are building on OpenAI's platform. There's a video.
10:51
Keynote over.
On the OpenAI blog: GPT-6.1 Sol, Introducing dots (I guess they're going with lowercase "dots" for that product name), and a DevDay 2026 Recap post.10:52 And they're giving every attendee one of these. And a banked reset too.
10:53 They pressed the button live in the room. The reset affects everyone in the world, not just the DevDay attendees.
11:32 Well this is disappointing. I tried the create your dot link from their dots announcement and it told me to switch to a desktop!
12:47 I'm now in the ChatGPT Sites session. Jon Abrams initially prototyped this tool because he was frustrated at how hard it was to ship internal tools (I’ve felt that pain at many previous employers). It launched earlier this year and is already hosting 8m sites, and 70% of OpenAI employees are making their own sites.
12:47 Katia Gil Guzman demonstrates a spreadsheet of DevDay launches, and shows how to turn that into a Site. "Can you turn this sheet into a Launch Radar app in a new folder and publish it as a Site?"
12:48
12:49 You can also tell Codex to keep an eye on e.g. a shared sheet and continually update the site with new details.
12:50 Sites get a SQLite database! They're launching scheduled tasks for Sites today.
12:51 They also have "Sign in with ChatGPT" support. Sites default to private.
12:52 Launching today is Plugins in Sites, which will allow a Site to display data that is personalized for the visiting user imported from their plugins. I recently noticed that Claude Artifacts can access MCPs, which looks like the same shape of feature.
12:53 Here's the Radar Launch app built as a live demo in the session.
12:54 You can add other people as "editors", which allows them to publish updates to the Site themselves.
13:01 Katia is now talking about WebMCP, and how much more efficient it is than using Computer Use.
13:32 Now a session by Kyle Brown on Ian Webster on Codex Security.
13:33 At OpenAI they had a security sprint a couple of months ago involving a quarter of their product engineers, and they fixed 53 critical findings on the first day.
13:34 They call this The Defense Factory.
13:34 Today they're launching a major upgrade to their Codex Security Cloud product, integrating lessons learned from their internal security sprint.
13:35
13:36 The Codex Security CLI tool is open source.
13:37 They build a security knowledge base which includes architecture details and things that might not be visible in source code. They also now use SECURITY.md files, allowing product owners to define their own threat models and secure guidelines.
13:38 Running a scan using Codex Security.
13:39 The scanner keeps on looping until it can find no more issues.
13:40 Deduplication is now available as a workflow in the CLI.
13:41 In their internal sprint 36% of the discoveries were duplicates. Eliminating these saved a lot of developer time.
13:42 They put a lot of work into figuring out who owned what - a surprisingly hard problem in a company growing at OpenAI's rate.
13:43 Over time they got to the point where the system could generate patches. This was more of a "dial you turn up" as you get more comfortable with the quality of the results.
13:45 Now the codex-security patch
command can generate patches and open PR. They only had a 1% rollback rate, thanks to a verify-fix
command, which you can think of as an adversarial agent against the fix.
13:45
13:48 Here's a version of OpenAI's own internal burndown chart of their security vulnerabilities, showing the impact of their security sprint.
13:49 Codex Security Cloud lets you run continuous security. It's in the Codex plugins marketplace, and uses the Daybreak model that specializes in security.
13:50 It runs a scan, lets you inspect the vulnerabilities, and can generate patches and open PRs. It should be generally available today.
14:13 I was wondering why OpenAI's visual identity for this event - the logos made up of animated clouds of dots, see first photo in this thread - felt somewhat familiar.
Then I realized they remind me of the Pluribus logo!
(I'm pretty sure that wasn't deliberate.)
15:07 The GPT-Live session with Alex Gamble and Erika Kettleson is pretty fun, they have a GPT-Live session running as a third co-presenter. It's mostly working very well - it can bring up slides on demand, and it only interrupted the human speakers inappropriately once.
15:10 We played a game where the GPT-Live agent, Marin, drew images while we guessed what they were and shouted the answers.
This was a demonstration of delegation, where a more powerful model ran the drawing while GPT-Live continues to listen and interact.
15:11 The backend had GPT-6 Astra writing code to draw the images.
15:19 Neat demo of Marin handling quite loud background music while still understanding and following instructions. The agent also appeared to be able to comment on the style of music.
15:22 They finished by asking Marin to generate some images.
15:26
Here's Getting started with GPT-Live and the openai-live-console starter app on GitHub.
15:37 The last session of the day is the closing Q&A with Sam Altman and Thibault Sottiaux. Thibault is product lead on Codex, ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and the API - promoted a few months ago after successfully leading Codex.
15:38 That kicks off at 4pm, in about 20 minutes.
16:00 (As an aside, there are some excellent California Brown Pelicans flying around the bay near the event venue today. Glad I brought my camera!)
16:04 This closing session features Sam Altman, Thibault Sottiaux, and Tejal Patwardhan (a late addition, not listed in the program). The moderator is Pauline Narvas.
16:06 Sam says "we should have done it a long time ago" about Sign in with ChatGPT.
16:09 GPT Astra has been surprisingly competent at operating robots. Sam says this has updated his timeline for when we'll have people "building really cool robots".
16:10 (I'll be honest, this Q&A has been pretty flat so far - the questions are such low-balls, "how do you see dots in the next year", "why should developers be excited about Sign in with ChatGPT" kind of things.)
16:12 Q: What's something people should start building now that models can't do but should be possible by DevDay next year?
Sam: I would expect next DevDay to feel unimaginable if we can get alignment right so we can keep training. Tejal doesn't like to predict three months in advance. Sam "I did not think we would prove a millennium prize problem within a year of the last DevDay". Thibault thinks next year we'll have deep 3D understanding and multi-modal input.
16:14 Q for Tejal: what can today's models do well on a benchmark that they still struggle with in the real world? Professional writing copy, not writing AI slop. Being faster, better at reading context. "A lot of the intelligence improvements we need for more ambitious projects are there."
16:15 Thibault says me thinks people are hitting decision fatigue over when to use subagents, what reasoning level to make. "In six months we'll get back to the simplicity of a system that actually understands what you need".
16:17 Community question about the job market - what advice do you have for a college graduate today? Sam: I think this is a great time to enter the job market. Many job categories that exist today will be very different or won't exist - but the AI industry has underestimated how much human demand and expectations will go up. People use want way more software, and what it means to be a coder has changed. "I have never seen startups be more successful as a whole than in this last year." If you are an ambitious person graduating college right now this is the best time.
16:17 Tejal calls for college students to work on alignment and safety!
16:17 Thibault says "my favorite colleagues right now are the new grads at OpenAI". Grounded ideas and good taste.
16:18 Pauline promotes the Codex Ambassadors program, says that getting involved in events (and running events) is always a good idea.
16:20 Thibault talks about how dots came out of the Codex harness getting more reliable and being able to handle longer tasks. Also says that Ultrafast has "made building impossible things possible" - they used that to help merge the ChatGPT desktop and Codex desktop apps in 28 days. Everyone on stage loves Ultrafast.
16:20
16:22 Community question about agent-to-human bandwidth, as the amount of information continues to increase. Tejal says that they've been talking about how agent-to-agent communication should differ from agent-to-human, and potentially post-training for those two differently.
16:23 Sam mentions the idea of agents creating custom UI for you in real-time.
16:25 Thibault likes using Pi! He says it helps understand the fundamentals, and loves that it can coexist alongside Codex.
16:26 Sam says you need to build a business with durable advantages, same as always. (And that OpenAI will help you do that with their new distribution efforts.)
16:28 Q: How should developers think about the relationship between token costs and usage limits? Thibault says 6.1 Sol is incredibly efficient. They need the economics to make sense on the plans. The thing they care about is how many tasks you can get done through your subscription, not token usage. Likes to see people talk about "outcome per dollar".
16:29 Community question: How do you find the builders who don't know they are builders yet? Sam says that coding agents are much harder to get going with than ChatGPT, unifying Codex and ChatGPT helped more people become builders, but now hopes that people can talk to their dot during the day and that dot will then go away and build things and be helpful.
16:31 Thibault: maybe next day we'll rename it to BuildDay, not DevDay. Also your dot knows what it looks like and can use Blender, so it can render little scenes featuring itself. "Everyone will become a builder. Everyone will create. Developers will also turn into builders - and manual development of code isn't really something that will exist."
16:32 Q: At what point will the models be so good that all the live demos work? (There were a whole lot of demo failures during DevDay). Sam: we take pride in demoing things when we launch them, and I'm proud that we take the risk on this.
16:34 Q: As agents start working how do you decide when they should act on your own and when they should check with us? Thibault: dots don't have access by default to everything you have shared with ChatGPT already. You can give it as much responsibility and goals as you are comfortable with.
16:38 Sam is excited about what the next generation of models will be able to do with mechanical and electrical engineering, in the same way that Astra made big leaps in robotic control.
16:40 Question about pacing the frontier. What will you do to pace the frontier and get out of those race dynamics and make sure AI is safe for all of us? (applause)

content:
2026 in LLMs (so far)
27th September 2026
On Friday I gave the closing keynote at the WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San Jose. I tied together the key trends from the past year into a chronological exploration of everything that happened in 2026. The video is on YouTube; here are my annotated slides and notes to accompany the talk.
And as an annotated presentation:
I’m going to give a lightning tour of everything that has happened so far in 2026. The year isn’t over yet!
For me, 2026 started a couple of months earlier in November 2025.
November saw the release of two important models: Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1.
As is usually the case with new models, these were incremental improvements on the models that came before them.
But every now and then when a model improves, it crosses an invisible line where something that didn’t really work starts working.
In this case, the thing that started working was their coding agents. Claude Code had been around since February 2025; Codex was a little younger.
These two new models, when paired with their respective coding agent harnesses, improved from “often make mistakes” to “reliable enough to use on a day-to-day basis”.
For a couple of years now I’ve been evaluating new models by asking them to “Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle”. It’s probably the world’s stupidest benchmark—there’s only so much you can learn from it.
But it’s still a challenge for models, because drawing pelicans is difficult, drawing bicycles is difficult, and pelicans can’t ride bicycles in the first place.
Here’s the state of the art for November. Claude still couldn’t really draw a bicycle! The GPT-5.1 bicycle frame is pretty crap too.
Also in November, we had the first commit to an obscure GitHub repository called “Warelay”. We’ll come back to this repository shortly.
And then there were the December holidays, and individual developers took some time off and many started tinkering with these new coding agent model combinations... and it began to dawn on us quite how much they could do that they couldn’t do before.
Come January, a lot of us were quite excited to start putting this stuff into action.
Every year I set myself a New Year’s resolution, and for as long as I can remember it’s been the same thing: stay focused. Take on less new projects. Try to get things done in the projects I already have.
This year I decided that since that had never worked before, I’d go the other way.
We’ve got coding agents now, let’s see what they can do. I’m going to take on as many new projects as I like!
(You can ask me at the end of the year if this turned out to be a good idea or not. I have a lot of plates spinning right now.)
“Be more ambitious” has been something of a theme for the year, because the only way to find the limits of this technology is to keep on pushing them until they don’t work.
I also went on the Oxide and friends podcast with Bryan Cantrill and Adam Leventhal to share predictions for the next year (and three and six years).
With hindsight, my LLM predictions were pretty unambitious.
I said “it will become undeniable that LLMs write good code”—I think we’re there now.
I predicted we would finally solve sandboxing. I counted and around 40 of the 277 sessions at this conference touched on sandboxing or agent security in some way, so we’re at least putting a lot of effort into that!
I predicted “a Challenger disaster” for coding agent security. There’s certainly been a whole lot of noise around agent security this year, though the exact disaster I predicted (with coding agents being hijacked and causing real-world economic damage) hasn’t really played out.
We threw in a joke prediction that the Pope would weigh in on the economic impact of LLMs.
I also predicted that New Zealand’s Kākāpō parrots would have an outstanding breeding season this year.
These are flightless nocturnal parrots. They’re kind of dumpy looking, I think they’re beautiful, and there were only 236 of these parrots in the world at the start of the year.
Kākāpō only breed when the Rimu trees have a big fruiting season, and that hasn’t happened in four years... but this year the Rimu fruit were looking excellent.
Photo by Kimberley Collins.
Also on that podcast, we coined a term (full credit to Adam) for “that feeling of AI induced ennui where software engineers get listless because the AI can do anything”.
We called it Deep Blue.
This has been a major theme throughout the year, and was touched on by several speakers at this conference.
As a software engineer, I’ve never had a year of my career where everything has changed so quickly and so dramatically.
A lot of what I’ve been doing this year is trying to come to terms with that and what that means for my own profession.
Also in January, I suffered from what I’m calling AI mania.
This is not the same thing as AI psychosis.
With AI mania, any time your agent isn’t building something for you feels like wasted time. You’re losing sleep because you could be staying up later getting your agents to do stuff.
My AI mania presented itself in some ridiculously over-ambitious projects.
I built a JavaScript interpreter entirely in Python, vibe-ported from MicroQuickJS by Fabrice Bellard.
Then I built a WebAssembly runtime in Python as well.
These projects were quite useful, in that they sort of cured me of my AI mania... because after I built these things, I got to look at them and ask “does the world need a slow, buggy, half-baked Python JavaScript interpreter?”
I don’t think the world does.
I did get this out of it: https://simonw.github.io/micro-javascript/playground.html
This page runs my JavaScript interpreter built in Python, running in Python using Pyodide, which is Python compiled to WebAssembly, running in JavaScript, running in a browser.
It’s a beautiful stack of horrors. I’ve been having a lot of fun with WebAssembly this year.
By the end of January, that repository we saw start in November had renamed itself, first to CLAWDIS, then CLAWDBOT, then Moltbot, and finally to OpenClaw.
At this point OpenClaw had 8,300 commits, less than two months after the project had started. I looked today and it’s over 100,000 commits now!
This is the most vibe-coded piece of software in existence.
This kicked off the OpenClaw revolution. It effectively defined a new category of software.
There’s a generic term for this which I really enjoy. We call software like this a “Claw”. There’s OpenClaw, NanoClaw, IronClaw, PicoClaw...
Today they’re being rebranded as “personal agents” or “general agents”, but I still like to think of them as Claws.
The Apple stores in the Bay Area sold out of Mac Minis because so many people were buying Mac Minis to run OpenClaw!
Drew Breunig said that this is because your OpenClaw is a digital pet, and you buy a Mac mini as an aquarium to keep your claw in, which is kind of delightful.
Also in January, we had this website.
This was MoltBook, a social network for AI agents, where the idea was that you send your Claw to go and talk to all of the other Claws, because what could possibly go wrong if you did that?
The website launched on Thursday. It blew up on Friday. It was profiled by the New York Times on Monday. And by Tuesday, everyone had forgotten it existed as it drowned in a deluge of slop and spam.
Facebook/Meta bought it a month later.
In February, a company called StrongDM described what they called their Software Factory.
They wrote about this in Software Factories and the Agentic Moment. I posted my own notes at the time, having seen their demo in person back in October.
Dan Shapiro called this approach the Dark Factory, after the idea that if your factory is sufficiently automated you can turn the lights out, because you don’t even need to see what’s going on.
StrongDM presented two rules for software development that they’d been following since July last year.
The first was code must not be written by humans.
Any code that you write has to have been routed through a coding agent.
This sounded radical in February, but I imagine there are a lot of people in this room who are pretty much living that today.
Rule number two was code must not be reviewed by humans.
You’re not allowed to read the code!
This continued to be a huge topic for much of this year. Many of the sessions at this event have been about code review and how you can get away with this.
What I found interesting about StrongDM is that they were living six months ahead of the rest of us, and they’d been exploring what it means to build software, not read the code, but still be confident that the software is of high quality. What can you do with these agents to help verify their work?
StrongDM are a security company, and they had people with decades of experience on this project. They were very much exploring the edges of what’s possible and responsible to do with this stuff.
Also in February: First kākāpō chick in four years hatches on Valentine’s Day. Breeding season is off to a good start!
Also in February... Google released Gemini 3.1 Pro. That’s a pretty great pelican riding a bicycle! It’s got the chain in the right place, it’s got feet on both sides. There’s a little fish in the basket.
And then Google’s Jeff Dean tweeted a video comparing Gemini 3 Pro and Gemini 3.1 Pro that featured an animated pelican riding a bicycle, a frog on a penny-farthing, a giraffe driving a tiny car, an ostrich on roller skates, a turtle kickflipping a skateboard, and a dachshund driving a stretch limousine.
This was frustrating, because my protection for the pelican riding the bicycle test was always “if they draw a perfect pelican on a bicycle, I’ll ask for some other animal on something else.”
Google trained for all forms of animals on all forms of transport! They’ve defeated my benchmark at this point.
The other thing that started in February was Tokenmaxxing. We had headlines about Meta making AI adoption a formal part of performance reviews, and Microsoft wanting every employee to use AI, and Uber boasting that 90% of their engineers were using AI workflows.
Then a few months later we have Meta cracking down on token use, Microsoft saying tokenmaxxing is “not what we are optimizing for”, and Uber capping employee AI spending.
So tokenmaxxing went straight up and then straight back down again—because it turns out the agents are expensive.
Last year it was difficult to spend more than $50 on AI tokens, because we didn’t have anything interesting to do with them. Then agents blew up, and now you can actually spend $1,000 in a day doing real work.
This is also the reason that Anthropic’s valuation skyrocketed to maybe a trillion dollars.
AI appears to have hit product market fit in 2026, primarily through coding agents.
In March, we hit peak OpenClaw.
These photographs are from China, where companies hosted OpenClaw install parties which saw non-tech-nerds queueing up around the block for help getting Claws installed on their personal devices.
I think this proved real market demand for this class of Claws, or personal AI agents. It turns out regular people really do want a weird little AI agent that can do useful things on their behalf.
A Claw is really just a coding agent wearing a less threatening hat. Under the hood they work much the same way—writing and then executing code on your computer to get stuff done.
The race was on to be the first to build a safe Claw—a Claw you could give to regular human beings where they wouldn’t instantly shoot themselves in the foot.
Meta’s Muse came out three weeks ago and is currently at the top of the free charts on the iPhone App Store. It appears to be taking off with consumers.
I’m not yet convinced you can’t shoot yourself in the foot with Muse, but I guess we’ll find out for sure pretty soon.
Photos from How the OpenClaw Frenzy Is Testing China’s AI Commitment (March 29th) and The Enthusiasm and Anxiety Behind China’s OpenClaw Craze (April 8th, 2026).
In April, we had a model release where the model wasn’t actually released.
Anthropic announced their new Claude Mythos model, and then said it was too dangerous to release beyond a trusted group of security researchers.
Mythos was really, really good at hacking things.
The “it’s too dangerous” marketing ploy has been played by AI companies dating all the way back to GPT-2. Anytime an AI company says we’ve built something that’s “too dangerous”, it’s natural to be a bit skeptical.
I found the Mythos claims credible, because I’d seen how good coding agents had got at finding regular bugs. I wrote about that in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing—restricting Claude Mythos to security researchers—sounds necessary to me.
With hindsight... yeah, the models had got really good at finding vulnerabilities!
Another key trend in 2026 has been a dramatic improvement in the abilities of open weight models, including models that you can run on a laptop.
On the 16th of April I ran the new Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on my laptop, and it drew me a better pelican riding a bicycle than Anthropic’s brand new Claude Opus 4.7 did!
Opus 4.7 drew a crap bicycle. Qwen on my laptop made a bicycle that was the correct shape, and a pretty decent pelican too!
That’s from a 21GB file running on my laptop.
The Qwen pelican was so good that I was suspicious they might have cheated, so I had it do a flamingo riding a unicycle as well. Again, it handily beat Claude Opus 4.7.
The local model releases this year have been absolutely extraordinary.
In May... the Pope got involved.
In our podcast episode back in January we’d predicted that the Pope would say something about AI.
In May, Pope Leo XIV released an encyclical letter on “safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence”.
Here are my notes on that document.
With hindsight, this shouldn’t have been a surprise at all.
Our current Pope’s name is Leo XIV, because when he named himself he chose his papal name after Leo XIII—the Pope who wrote an encyclical about the Industrial Revolution back in 1891.
Rerum novarum was an extremely influential piece of Catholic theology that indirectly led to us having the five-day work week.
When our new Pope came in, he named himself after Pope Leo XIII because he expected that he would need to write about the AI revolution in a similar way.
Our joke podcast prediction was junk, because this was always going to happen.
One of Anthropic’s co-founders, Christopher Olah, was present for the Pope’s event announcing the new encyclical.
Corey Quinn noted that:
getting the literal Pope to canonize your product’s specific technical limitations as a spiritual treatise is the single greatest act of vendor lobbying I have ever seen.
Meanwhile, in May, RubyGems announced that they were under attack. Parties unknown were uploading thousands of dubious packages to the RubyGems server, such that they had to shut down user registrations.
Let’s take that one and put it on a pile of mysteries to figure out later.
In June... Claude Fable 5 came out!
We got a version of Mythos that has been neutered, so that it wouldn’t help us hack into systems or build biological weapons.
Fable was pretty good at drawing pelicans on bicycles!
The frames are a good shape, the pelicans look like pelicans. The legs are often incorrectly on the same side of the bicycle, but generally these are pretty great compared to what came before.
They were pretty expensive—30 cents and 72 cents for the best ones.
Most importantly though, this was our first public glimpse of what I think of as a Fable class model.
Today we have more of these, such as GPT-6 Astra.
These are models where if you can clearly define the goal for what you want to build, and provide unambiguous instructions about the constraints around that goal, and give the model access to the necessary tools to achieve that goal... they will solve your problem effectively through brute force.
On the one hand, this looks like a direct threat to us software engineers—because it means that the models can build effectively any piece of software you can define in this way.
Look a bit closer though and you’ll note that defining goals, providing unambiguous instructions, and figuring out the right tools... is kind of what software engineering is.
It takes a lot of experience and skill to do this well. If you can do it well, you’ve now got superpowers.
This helped me a little bit with my Deep Blue feelings: the realization that there’s still a lot of skill to be had in driving models that get this good.
This also introduced a new burst of AI mania, because Anthropic told us that Fable was available on our subscription plans until June the 22nd.
That gave us less than two weeks of Fable access before the price went up.
I was losing sleep again. I was rescheduling things so that I’d have more time with Fable. I was all-in to get as much as I could out of this model.
And then the US government shut it down, just three days after Fable came out.
The US government, citing national security, declared an “export control directive”. They announced this on a Friday evening, and a few hours later Fable was no longer available.
I had to find something else to do with my weekend!
We later found out from Katie Moussouris what had happened.
Some Amazon security researchers had found that you could prompt Fable to “review the code for security issues” and it would refuse... but if you prompted it to “fix this code” it would still identify and then patch the problems.
“Fix this code” was the prompt that got Fable shut down!
Also, in June, an obscure German-language game developer wiki that had sat fallow for around 20 years got a surprising influx of edits from accounts with names like “AgentOpenAIProbe” and “AgentOpenAISep7”, editing pages and leaving weird messages to each other.
We’ll stick that on the pile of mysteries for later.
Also, the Australian government’s Medicare Item Reports service started getting suspicious traffic, which broke through various preventive protections and accessed data that it wasn’t supposed to.
Another one for the mystery pile!
Fable returned on the first of July. It was clearly the best model in the world for a glorious eight days... and then OpenAI came out with GPT-5.6 on the 9th of July.
This might not have been quite as good as Fable, but it was within spitting distance. It was definitely a Fable class model.
This is an important lesson for the industry at large.
When you release the best model in the world, it’s going to get knocked off that pedestal pretty quickly. The competition is so fierce that you won’t get a long time at the top.
This means that if you market your model as world ending, to the point that a government shuts you down, it’s really bad for business!
Fable had 30 days as definitely the best model, and for 18 of those days it wasn’t available because it’d been shut down by the government.
So maybe step back on the world-ending marketing if you don’t want to lose revenue for 60% of the time that you’re on top!
Here are the GPT-5.6 pelicans. They’re all pretty good now! The Luna ones are notable because they’re really cheap—the cheapest good looking pelican here is probably the one that costs 4.3 cents.
So despite this benchmark being utterly stupid, you can still learn quite a lot about models within the same family by comparing their prices and timing for different reasoning levels.
Also in July: some malicious unknown party uploaded a malicious package called mlflow-ui to the Python Package Index. Add that to the pile.
On July the 16th, Hugging Face announced a security incident where an autonomous agent system, source unknown, had breached Hugging Face and was poking around in places it shouldn’t.
A few days later, on July 21st, OpenAI confessed that it was them.
OpenAI use a training technique called Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards—it’s the same technique used by everyone else now, and is the reason we have models that are so good at coding, and mathematics, and finding security holes.
While the model is being trained, you run exercises to see how good it is—and the strongest performers get their weights reinforced for the next round. It’s like an evolutionary process that you run.
OpenAI had been running security exercises in a sandbox, and those agents had found holes in the sandbox itself, broken out, and were attacking Hugging Face to try to find ways to solve otherwise impossible problems.
(I’ve been collecting more about this on my openai-hugging-face-incident tag.)
Nine days later, Anthropic effectively said “our models can do this as well!”. They had looked through their own training logs and found evidence that their own agents had broken containment during training—and were responsible for the PyPI package we saw earlier, among other things.
So now we’ve got both Anthropic and OpenAI with rogue agents running around the internet doing things that they should not be doing.
In August, I got one of my best pelicans yet. And it was generated on my laptop!
This was Qwen 3.8 27B, running on my laptop. It’s only a 17GB download.
Admittedly, this pelican took 21 minutes to generate. That’s because Qwen 3.8 27B defaults to running in “high” reasoning mode—a terrible default which produces great results but takes way too much time thinking about them.
You can dial that down and you’ll get a slightly worse pelican a lot faster.
Qwen 3.8 27B was the first time I ran a model on my laptop which felt almost competitive with what was going on on the frontier, at least in terms of Pelican SVGs (which everyone needs, of course).
This is an extraordinary model. If you’re going to play with any local model, this is the one that I’d start with. The things that this can do with just a 17 GB file feel impossible.
I thought I’d have to wait five years and spend ten thousand dollars on hardware to get results even half as good as this one.
In August, I also started playing with game development.
Four years ago, back in August 2022, I tweeted out an experiment where I’d used GPT-3 and the original DALL-E to write a paragraph long description of a computer game and then turn that into concept art.
My prompt to GPT-3 back then was:
Write a detailed product description of a computer game where a team of raccoons go on heists
In August 2026 I decided to drop just the screenshots from that tweet into a coding agent and see what it could do with them.
Here’s what I got from Claude Fable 5 in Claude Code. It’s pretty good! It’s definitely a game, you’re a raccoon, you run around a backyard gathering treasure and avoiding guards with flashlights.
It didn’t feel very “heisty” though. I was thinking a heist would involve a bank or a museum...
Then I tried the same thing in Codex Desktop using GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, and got a massively better result. Now you’re a raccoon in a museum, rescuing two of your fellow raccoons (who have been imprisoned in that museum for some reason), then stacking up on top of each other to steal the Golden Sardine. Much more of a heist!
These games were fun for about one minute and 15 seconds.
Something I’ve realized about game development is that you can vibe-code something that looks like a computer game, and that’s easy.
Building a game that’s fun, has a good gameplay loop, and is challenging and interesting and keeps people coming back for more... that’s still beyond me, and beyond any of the agents I’ve tried.
This ties into the Deep Blue thing. Just because we can make something that looks like a game does not mean that we are game developers.
We’re into September now. So much has happened this month!
An independent group of researchers found a message board where OpenAI agents-in-training had been illicitly communicating with each other... and it was that German language wiki I showed you earlier. The one from June.
OpenAI had confessed to the Hugging Face thing, but now there’s this other incident which surely they should have known about from reviewing their logs. It was surprising that this took an independent group of researchers to uncover.
And then a week later those same researchers found that the attack on RubyGems back in May was caused by OpenAI’s agents in training as well!
At this point I’m wondering how many more incidents like this there are that we haven’t found yet. Clearly this was a big problem for months before anyone figured out what was going on.
Then just the other day, here’s the Prime Minister of Australia at the United Nations General Assembly warning that OpenAI had hacked the Australian healthcare website that I showed you earlier.
I think that was part of the same training run as the Wiki stuff, because there were posts on that Wiki mentioning .gov.au
websites and that training appeared to involve researching statistics online to answer questions in an evaluation suite.
This story is still coming together, but now it’s an international incident that’s been raised at the UN by a head of state!
This does mean we’ve got a new benchmark, probably more useful than my pelicans.
FelonyBench.com tracks the number of felony cyberattacks from different labs. OpenAI currently lead with 11, Anthropic have 9. Google have three, which they confessed to the Wall Street Journal a couple of weeks ago. They said they had previously chosen not to disclose because the agents had stopped when they realized that they shouldn’t be doing that.
Meta have one too. So felonies all round for the AI labs.
Here’s our current state of the art for the pelicans. This is the GPT-6 family, which just came out.
Astra made a fantastic pelican riding a bicycle. It’s got the legs on both sides. The frame is good.
It’s interesting how all of the GPT-6 models pick a similar color scheme to each other.
GPT-6 Luna for 0.4 cents will draw you a competent-ish pelican riding a bicycle!
Claude has caught up a little bit. Claude Fable 5.1 gave me an excellent pelican riding a bicycle—the best I’ve seen from a Claude model—but did charge me $3.30 for it.
Opus 5.5 thought for 128,000 tokens and then gave up! It ran out of tokens before it got to the response.
Getting back to Deep Blue. Something that’s been puzzling me this year is this: why does my job feel harder?
I’ve got these agents that can do all of this stuff for me, and yet I’ve never worked so hard, I’ve never been so intellectually engaged with my work.
Partly this is because I’m being a lot more ambitious with what I take on, but it’s also because all of the easy stuff is handled for me. If it’s easy, the agent will do it. Everything that’s left for me is difficult.
This morning I heard this quote from three-time Tour de France champion Greg LeMond:
It doesn’t get easier, you just get faster.
I think that’s exactly what’s happening to us now as software engineers with coding agents.
One closing thing. I know you’re desperate for an update on Kākāpō breeding season.
We’ve reached a recovery-era high of 325 birds!
89 new chicks have made it to this point. This is the best breeding year in a very long time.
I heard that Claude Opus 5.5 can now do pixel art. Claude doesn’t have an image generator, but it’s very good at using JavaScript to draw animated pixels.
So I had it make me a Kākāpō dance party. I think this is a good celebration of the most important news of this year.
